resolved_by: The Supreme Court resolved the split in United States v. Taylor, 596 U.S. 845 (2022), holding that attempted Hobbs Act robbery is not a crime of violence under § 924(c) because the attempt must itself involve actual, attempted, or threatened force.
issue: Is an attempt to commit a crime of violence automatically a crime of violence under § 924(c), or must the attempt itself involve the attempted use, threatened use, or actual use of force?

sides.position: An attempt to commit a crime of violence is invariably a crime of violence, even where the completed offense can be committed by threatened force alone.
cases: United States v. Walker, 990 F.3d 316 (3d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Smith, 957 F.3d 590 (5th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Ingram, 947 F.3d 1021 (7th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Dominguez, 954 F.3d 1251 (9th Cir. 2020)
United States v. St. Hubert, 909 F.3d 335 (11th Cir. 2018)

sides.position: An attempt to commit a crime of violence is not automatically a crime of violence; the attempt must involve attempted force, and an attempt to threaten force does not constitute an attempt to use force.
cases: United States v. Taylor, 979 F.3d 203 (4th Cir. 2020), aff'd, 596 U.S. 845 (2022)
United States v. Greene, No. 21-4349 (4th Cir. 2024)

this_court: Follows the Taylor rule that an attempt must itself involve attempted force, consistent with the Supreme Court's resolution in Taylor.
quote: Our decision in Taylor created a split with our sister circuits, and the Supreme Court promptly took up the case.
cite: United States v. Xavier Greene, No. 21-4349 (4th Cir. 2024)
